title: Acquire Infrastructure: DNS Server
summary: Rather than hijacking someone else's name resolution, an adversary builds and operates a DNS server, the service that answers lookups of names to addresses, for their own operation. The parent technique covers infrastructure acquisition in general; this sub-technique is specifically about owning the answering service. Control of the authoritative server lets the operator return different answers to different queries, so a malware sample can receive a unique address while ordinary lookups are refused or answered normally. That flexibility supports DNS tunnelling, domain generation algorithms, and fallback logic in implants. The observable footprint sits on the attacker's side rather than the victim's: name server records that point to cheap hosting, very low query volume before an operation starts, wildcard records, unusual or non-standard port 53 behaviour, and provider abuse reports. From a defender's vantage point the same activity looks like DNS traffic, so the practical separation comes from query patterns such as long encoded labels, high-entropy subdomains, and repeated lookups of domains registered days earlier.

beginner.definition: A DNS server is the internet service that turns a website name into the number a computer needs. Most people use someone else's. In this sub-technique the attacker sets up and runs their own DNS server instead. It is the same idea as the parent technique, but the thing acquired is the answering service itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: When an attacker runs the DNS server, they decide what answers infected machines receive. They can hide the real location of their control server behind a changing address. They can also answer only the machines they want and ignore everyone else, which makes the setup very hard to find.
howItWorks: The attacker registers a domain and buys a small cloud server or space on an existing name service.
They install DNS software such as BIND or PowerDNS, which answers name lookups.
They create records that point chosen names to their own control servers.
They configure the server to answer some queries normally and refuse or ignore others.
The malware asks for a crafted name and receives data hidden in the reply, or a fresh address.
Records are edited between operations so old names die and new ones appear.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel switchboard. A normal operator looks up a guest and connects the call. A corrupt operator answers only callers who use a special code word, and for everyone else says no such guest exists. The switchboard is real, so nobody suspects the building.
takeaways: Traffic to a domain does not prove the owner is legitimate.
Long or random-looking subdomain names in queries are a classic warning sign.
Watching query volume and record changes catches this setup faster than watching ports.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent Acquire Infrastructure technique.
Describe how a self-managed DNS server supports command and control.
Identify the query patterns that suggest DNS tunnelling or conditional answers.
Recognise the provider and registration artefacts that point to hostile name servers.
Describe how defenders baseline normal DNS behaviour to find anomalies.
